e-622.knowledge_point: Finding the Velocity Vector Given the Acceleration Vector
e-622.problem:
The acceleration $\mathbf{a}$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
\mathbf{a}(t) = \langle 10, 0\rangle.
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $\mathbf{v} = \langle 10,20\rangle$ when $t=1,$ calculate the velocity vector of $P$ at time $t.$
e-622.worked_solution:
To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨10,0⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 10\,\text{d}t,\int 0\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨10t+{C}_{1},\,{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $\mathbf{v} (1)= \langle 10,20\rangle.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨10(1)+{C}_{1},\,{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨10,20⟩ & =⟨10+{C}_{1},\,{C}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}10 & =10+{C}_{1} \\ {C}_{1} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
C_2 = 20.
$$

Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨10t,\,20⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1

The acceleration a at time t of a particle P moving in the xy-plane is given by a=⟨2t,1−2t⟩. Given that the particle has velocity v=⟨0,0⟩ when t=1, calculate the velocity vector of P at time t.

a
v=⟨t2,2+t−t2⟩
b
v=⟨3t2−1,2t−t2⟩
c
v=⟨2t2−1,2t−t2⟩
d
v=⟨t2−1,t−t2⟩
e
v=⟨t2−1,2+t−2t2⟩
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating componentwise gives v(t)=⟨t²+C₁,t−t²+C₂⟩. The condition v(1)=⟨0,0⟩ yields C₁=−1 and C₂=0, so option d is correct.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a=⟨2t,1-2t⟩.
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨0,0⟩$ when $t=1$, calculate the velocity vector of $P$ at time $t.$
after.worked_solution:
To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨2t,1-2t⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 2t\,\text{d}t,\int (1-2t)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{2}+{C}_{1},t-{t}^{2}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(1)=⟨0,0⟩.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨{1}^{2}+{C}_{1},1-{1}^{2}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨0,0⟩ & =⟨1+{C}_{1},{C}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =1+{C}_{1} \\ {C}_{1} & =-1,\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & ={C}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
v=⟨{t}^{2}-1,t-{t}^{2}⟩.
$$

Question 1

The acceleration a at time t of a particle P moving in the xy-plane is given by a=⟨2t,1−2t⟩. Given that the particle has velocity v=⟨0,0⟩ when t=1, calculate the velocity vector of P at time t.

a
v=⟨t2,2+t−t2⟩
b
v=⟨3t2−1,2t−t2⟩
c
v=⟨2t2−1,2t−t2⟩
d
v=⟨t2−1,t−t2⟩
e
v=⟨t2−1,2+t−2t2⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector: v(t)=∫a(t)dt=∫⟨2t,1−2t⟩dt=⟨∫2tdt,∫(1−2t)dt⟩=⟨t2+C1,t−t2+C2⟩

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that v(1)=⟨0,0⟩. Substituting t=1, we get v(1)=⟨12+C1,1−12+C2⟩⟨0,0⟩=⟨1+C1,C2⟩.

So, we must have 0=1+C1C1=−1,

and 0=C2.

Therefore, the velocity vector is v=⟨t2−1,t−t2⟩.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Velocity Vector Given the Acceleration Vector
content.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a=⟨2t,1-2t⟩.
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨0,0⟩$ when $t=1$, calculate the velocity vector of $P$ at time $t.$
content.worked_solution:
To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨2t,1-2t⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 2t\,\text{d}t,\int (1-2t)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{2}+{C}_{1},t-{t}^{2}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(1)=⟨0,0⟩.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨{1}^{2}+{C}_{1},1-{1}^{2}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨0,0⟩ & =⟨1+{C}_{1},{C}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =1+{C}_{1} \\ {C}_{1} & =-1,\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & ={C}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
v=⟨{t}^{2}-1,t-{t}^{2}⟩.
$$

The acceleration a at time t of a particle P moving in the xy-plane is given by a=⟨cos⁡t,sin⁡t⟩. Given that the particle has velocity v=⟨22,−22⟩ when t=π4, calculate the velocity vector of P at time t.

a
v=⟨−sin⁡t,2cos⁡t⟩
b
v=⟨sin⁡t,−cos⁡t⟩
c
v=⟨2sin⁡t,cos⁡t⟩
d
v=⟨−sin⁡t,2cos⁡t⟩
e
v=⟨2sin⁡t,cos⁡t⟩
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating acceleration gives v(t)=⟨sin t+C₁,−cos t+C₂⟩. At t=π/4, the given velocity implies C₁=C₂=0. Thus option b satisfies both the acceleration and initial velocity.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟩$ when $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$, calculate the velocity vector of $P$ at time $t.$
after.worked_solution:
To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t,\int \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{C}_{1},-\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(\frac{\pi }{4})=⟨\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟩.$ 
Substituting $t=\frac{\pi }{4},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})+{C}_{1},-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟩ & =⟨\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+{C}_{1},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+{C}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+{C}_{1} \\ {C}_{1} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+{C}_{2} \\ {C}_{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
v=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩.
$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Velocity Vector Given the Acceleration Vector
content.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟩$ when $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$, calculate the velocity vector of $P$ at time $t.$
content.worked_solution:
To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t,\int \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{C}_{1},-\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(\frac{\pi }{4})=⟨\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟩.$ 
Substituting $t=\frac{\pi }{4},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})+{C}_{1},-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟩ & =⟨\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+{C}_{1},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+{C}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+{C}_{1} \\ {C}_{1} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+{C}_{2} \\ {C}_{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
v=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩.
$$
